explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The verse says it plainly: "the Day of the LORD is near." Then it describes that day as "a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations." I think that's why Ezekiel is told to wail. Nobody wails over a day they're looking forward to.

I get why it caught your eye, friend. It sounds like a serious day too. But Ezekiel's message never mentions it. The verse names "the Day of the LORD" and says it will be "a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations."

That one sounds like a nice day, friend, and that's the giveaway. This message isn't nice at all. The day Ezekiel names is "the Day of the LORD," and the verse calls it "a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations." Firstfruits never shows up in these verses.

Hold on, baker, let's check the verse. It doesn't promise peace anywhere. It says "a time of doom for the nations." So the answer is False. If you were hoping for a calm day, you'd want a different prophecy.
Right, baker. The verse says the day "will be a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations." Doom is the opposite of peace. This is not a message you'd stitch onto a pillow.

Yes, baker. The verse says "there will be anguish in Cush when the slain fall in Egypt." Cush is Egypt's neighbor to the south, so the news doesn't stay in Egypt. It travels, and it hurts all along the way.

I know, friend, when a big neighbor falls, you might expect some people to throw a party. But the verse says the opposite. When the slain fall in Egypt, "there will be anguish in Cush." Nobody in Cush is passing out party hats.

Laughter is my department, baker, and this isn't the place for it. The verse says "there will be anguish in Cush when the slain fall in Egypt." That's a heavy moment. Anguish is the word God gives Ezekiel.

That's the word, baker. God says, "her proud strength will collapse." Egypt's allies fall first, and then the strength Egypt was proud of goes down too. Picture a tall stack of cookie boxes with the bottom one pulled out.
That would be good news for Egypt, friend, and this message has none. God says her allies will fall and "her proud strength will collapse." Nothing in this verse comes back. It all goes down.

Doubling sounds great, baker, but that's not this verse. God says the allies of Egypt will fall, and "her proud strength will collapse." It's the opposite of getting bigger. Nobody here is getting a second helping of strength.

Exactly, baker. God says, "Then they will know that I am the LORD…" when He sets fire to Egypt and her helpers are shattered. That line comes back again and again in this chapter. God wants them to know who He is, and that's what this is about.
Babylon does show up in this chapter, friend, but not in this verse. Here God says, "Then they will know that I am the LORD…" The knowing is about who God is. It isn't about any king.

Nice try, friend, but the verse never says that. It says, "Then they will know that I am the LORD…" God is the one acting, so it's God they will know. A little later in the chapter, He says He will destroy the idols (Ezekiel 30:13).

explanations.answer: To frighten Cush out of complacency
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The verse says God's messengers go out in ships "to frighten Cush out of complacency." Complacency means feeling too settled to worry. Those ships are headed straight for Cush, and I think it's going to be a wake-up call.

explanations.answer: To call Cush to come help Egypt
explanations.explanation: That makes sense, friend, but it's not what the verse says. These messengers go out from God "to frighten Cush out of complacency." And earlier, Cush is named among those who will fall with Egypt by the sword (Ezekiel 30:5). This isn't a recruiting trip.

explanations.answer: To carry off the wealth of Cush
explanations.explanation: Wealth does come up in this chapter, baker, but not here. The verse says the messengers go out "to frighten Cush out of complacency." Earlier it says Egypt's wealth is taken away (Ezekiel 30:4). These ships are carrying a warning, not cargo.

That's right, baker. God says, "He and his people with him, the most ruthless of the nations, will be brought in to destroy the land." Nebuchadnezzar is the king of Babylon. When God uses that kind of description, it tells you what Egypt is facing.

The verse actually says it, baker. God says, "He and his people with him, the most ruthless of the nations, will be brought in to destroy the land." The "he" is Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon. So the answer is True.
That's right, baker. God says, "I will make the streams dry up." Streams are what keep a land going, so this is a serious thing to say. It's one more way God shows He isn't done.
I see where your mind went, friend. But this verse says something different. God says, "I will make the streams dry up." No blood in this one.
Close on the water, friend, but you've got the wrong direction. God says, "I will make the streams dry up." Not overflow, but dry up. Nothing is rushing in here, it's all going away.

Yes, baker. God says, "By the hands of foreigners I will bring desolation upon the land and everything in it." Right before that, He says He will sell the land to the wicked. Then He ends with "I, the LORD, have spoken."

Good guess for a royal kind of word, friend, but it's not this verse. God says, "By the hands of foreigners I will bring desolation upon the land and everything in it." Princes come up in the next verses, and not in a good way. God says there will no longer be a prince in Egypt (Ezekiel 30:13).

I can see why it sounds right, baker. But this verse doesn't mention priests at all. God says, "By the hands of foreigners I will bring desolation upon the land and everything in it." The word is foreigners.
Let's look at the verse again, baker. God says, "There will no longer be a prince in Egypt." So the answer is False. He also says He will instill fear in that land.
That's right, baker. God says, "There will no longer be a prince in Egypt, and I will instill fear in that land." The land is losing its prince. It's not a small thing.
Yes, baker. God says, "I will instill fear in that land." It comes right after He says there will no longer be a prince in Egypt. The word is fear, and the verse stays with it.
That would be a nice ending, friend, but it isn't this one. God says, "I will instill fear in that land." Peace is not what this verse is handing out.
I'd love to give you that one, baker. But the verse says the opposite. God says, "I will instill fear in that land." There's no hope in this line.
That's it, baker. God says, "A cloud will cover her." It comes right after the day is darkened in Tahpanhes. The cloud echoes the "day of clouds" from the start of the chapter.
Water does get a lot of attention in this chapter, friend, but not here. The verse says, "A cloud will cover her." The cover is a cloud, and it matches the darkened day in Tahpanhes.
A swarm would cover a lot, baker, but it's not what the verse says. God says, "A cloud will cover her." Just a cloud, and I think that's a heavy enough picture on its own.

That's right, baker. God says, "I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt." He adds that it "has not been bound up for healing, or splinted for strength to hold the sword." Nobody has even set it.

I get the guess, friend, but this verse is about something else. God says, "I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt." The splint question is about holding the sword, and a sword goes in an arm.
Funny guess, baker, but the verse points somewhere else. God says, "I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt." It mentions a splint for strength "to hold the sword," and that's an arm job.

explanations.answer: The strong arm and the broken one
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. God says, "I will break his arms, both the strong one and the one already broken." That means both are going. After that, the sword falls from his hand.
Almost, friend, but God says more. He says, "I will break his arms, both the strong one and the one already broken." So the arm that's still strong is included too.
That's half of it, baker. God says, "I will break his arms, both the strong one and the one already broken." So the broken one gets broken more, and the strong one gets broken too.

That's right, baker. God says He "will make the sword fall from his hand." It ties back to the arm that couldn't be splinted "for strength to hold the sword." Without strong arms, that sword isn't staying in his hand.
A scepter sounds right for a king, friend, but it's not in this verse. God says He "will make the sword fall from his hand." The verse before talks about holding the sword too.
I see the thinking, baker, but this verse doesn't mention a bow. God says He "will make the sword fall from his hand." It's a sword from start to finish.

Yes, baker. God says, "I will strengthen the arms of Babylon's king and place My sword in his hand." So while Pharaoh's arms are breaking, the king of Babylon's arms are getting stronger. Two kings, two very different directions.

The verse says it right out, baker. God says, "I will strengthen the arms of Babylon's king and place My sword in his hand." So the answer is True. Meanwhile, He says He will break the arms of Pharaoh.
That's right, baker. God says He will break the arms of Pharaoh, "who will groan before him like a mortally wounded man." I think this one is a heavy picture. It's a sober way to end the passage.

The verse does say it, baker. God says He will break the arms of Pharaoh, "who will groan before him like a mortally wounded man." So the answer is True. I think this is a heavy line, and it should be read slowly.
